plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 1: Structure and Bonding
plan.contextChunk: This figure sets a geometric solid beside a chemical structure to establish a drawing convention, using four images across one horizontal band. At the left are two magenta line drawings of a four-faced solid: the first a plain outline with one front edge thickened, the second adding black interior edges, one solid and one dashed, that run from the top vertex and a side vertex to the center. The pair is labeled "A regular tetrahedron". At the right, a carbon written as "C" carries four hydrogens written as "H": one directly above and one to the right on ordinary thin lines, one to the left on a short dashed line, and one below on a heavy black wedge that widens away from the carbon. Three leader arrows name these bond types as "Bonds in plane of page", "Bond receding into page", and "Bond coming out of plane". A ball-and-stick model at the far right shows a dark gray central sphere with four pale hydrogen spheres on light rods, and a curly brace groups the notation and the model under "A tetrahedral carbon atom". Aligning solid, flat notation, and model lets the reader read wedges and dashes as depth cues rather than as different kinds of bonds, the shorthand used for three-dimensional structures throughout organic chemistry.

interactions.teaches: The learner connects each 2D drawing convention to a real 3D direction: thin lines are bonds in the page plane, dashed bonds recede behind the page, and solid wedges project out toward the viewer.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Overall layout is a single horizontal textbook-style band about 10.5 world units wide by 3.2 high. Use a white background and mostly black typography. Left group occupies x≈[-5.0,-1.8], right carbon/model group occupies x≈[-0.6,5.0]. Use +X screen-right, +Y screen-up, +Z coming out of the page toward the viewer; negative Z is into the page. The left plain tetrahedron is centered near (-4.55,0.3,0), about 1.25 units wide and 1.35 units tall in the screen plane. Draw magenta edges in #ff0088: apex at local (0,0.75,0), left vertex (-0.65,-0.15,0), right vertex (0.65,-0.20,0), lower/front vertex (-0.18,-0.95,0). Edges include apex-left, apex-right, left-right, left-lower/front, right-lower/front, and apex-lower/front. The apex-to-lower/front edge is thickened to about 4x the normal line width. The second tetrahedron is centered near (-2.65,0.3,0), same vertices and magenta wireframe. Add black orientation cues: a heavy solid black wedge/edge from near the carbon-center point toward the lower/front vertex, a short black dashed line from the left vertex toward the center to indicate recession, and a thin black line from the center toward the right vertex for an in-plane bond. Caption under both tetrahedra at y≈-1.25, bold, two lines: A regular / tetrahedron. The flat carbon notation is centered at (0.65,0.15,0). Letter C at origin of the notation. H above at (0.65,0.95,0) connected by a thin vertical line; H right at (1.25,0.05,0) connected by a thin line angled slightly down-right; H left at (0.02,-0.02,0) connected by a dashed line angled slightly down-left; H lower-left at (0.52,-0.72,0) connected by a black filled wedge from a narrow point at C to a wider end near the H. Place the label Bond receding into page above-left of the notation around (-1.05,1.55,0), with a leader arrow down-right to the dashed bond. Place Bonds in plane of page above/right around (1.75,1.8,0), with two leader arrows to the vertical and right thin bonds. Place Bond coming out of plane below/right around (1.95,-0.85,0), with a leader arrow to the wedge bond. The ball-and-stick model is centered near (4.1,0.25,0). Carbon sphere radius ≈0.28, color dark gray #4d4d4d. Hydrogen spheres radius ≈0.20, color pale ivory/gray #d8d8c2 with glossy shading. Bond cylinders radius ≈0.055, color light steel gray #aeb8c6. Approximate hydrogen positions relative to carbon: upper in-plane H at (-0.08,0.78,0.00), right in-plane H at (0.78,0.05,0.00), left/receding H at (-0.65,0.18,-0.45), lower/front H at (-0.22,-0.68,0.55). The dashed flat bond should map to the left/receding 3D bond; the solid wedge should map to the lower/front 3D bond; the two thin bonds should map to the upper and right 3D bonds. Curly brace spans from x≈0.0 to x≈5.0 below the notation/model at y≈-1.25, with centered caption A tetrahedral / carbon atom at y≈-1.7. When a category is selected, color its leader text/arrow, flat bond mark, and matching 3D cylinder/sphere halo with a shared glow color: in-plane blue #2d7ff9, receding purple #7b4dff, coming-out orange #ff9900. Nonselected bonds remain black/gray but slightly dimmed.
interactionPlan.notes: Render labels and leader arrows as screen-facing text and line/arrow overlays anchored to world points so they remain readable. The click targets should include each leader label, the corresponding flat bond mark, and the matching 3D bond/cylinder; clicking any of them selects that orientation category. For the solid wedge, use a filled triangular mesh in the page plane with its narrow point at carbon and wide base near the lower H. For the dashed receding bond, use short line segments rather than a continuous stroke. Use emissive material or an outline/glow postprocess for the selected 3D bond and selected hydrogen endpoint. Keep the flat notation nearly front-on while the ball-and-stick model uses true 3D coordinates to show the same tetrahedral directions.

authoredContext:
A representation of a tetrahedral carbon atom is shown in the figure. Note the conventions used to show three-dimensionality: solid lines represent bonds in the plane of the page, the heavy wedged line represents a bond coming out of the page toward the viewer, and the dashed line represents a bond receding back behind the page, away from the viewer. Get used to them; these representations will be used throughout the text.

A representation of van’t Hoff’s tetrahedral carbon atom. The solid lines represent bonds in the plane of the paper, the heavy wedged line represents a bond coming out of the plane of the page toward the viewer, and the dashed line represents a bond going back behind the plane of the page away from the viewer.

Two regular tetrahedrons (one with 3 D representation), the wedge-bond structure, and ball and stick model of a tetrahedral carbon atom.

Why, though, do atoms bond together, and how can chemical bonds be described electronically? The why question is relatively easy to answer: atoms bond together because the compound that results is more stable and lower in energy than the separate atoms. Energy—usually as heat—is always released and flows out of the chemical system when a bond forms. Conversely, energy is added to the chemical system when a bond breaks. Making bonds always releases energy, and breaking bonds always absorbs energy. The how question is more difficult. To answer it, we need to know more about the electronic properties of atoms.

At the left are two magenta line drawings of a four-faced solid: the first a plain outline with one front edge thickened, the second adding black interior edges, one solid and one dashed, that run from the top vertex and a side vertex to the center. The pair is labeled "A regular tetrahedron". At the right, a carbon written as "C" carries four hydrogens written as "H": one directly above and one to the right on ordinary thin lines, one to the left on a short dashed line, and one below on a heavy black wedge that widens away from the carbon. Three leader arrows name these bond types as "Bonds in plane of page", "Bond receding into page", and "Bond coming out of plane". A ball-and-stick model at the far right shows a dark gray central sphere with four pale hydrogen spheres on light rods, and a curly brace groups the notation and the model under "A tetrahedral carbon atom". Aligning solid, flat notation, and model lets the reader read wedges and dashes as depth cues rather than as different kinds of bonds, the shorthand used for three-dimensional structures throughout organic chemistry.
